easy.question: Who is asked to listen to Moses’ words?
answers: The heavens and the earth
The mountains and rivers
The priests and elders
easy.explanation: Moses calls on the heavens to listen and the earth to hear.

easy.question: What are Moses’ words compared to in verse 2?
answers: Fire and wind
Rain, dew, and showers
Stones and dust
easy.explanation: Moses compares his teaching to rain, dew, and showers that water plants.

easy.question: What should be given to God after His name is proclaimed?
answers: Many gifts
A new land
Greatness and honor
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Ascribe ye greatness unto our God.”

medium.question: What is the connection between proclaiming God’s name and giving Him greatness?
answers: Proclaiming His name leads people to recognize His greatness
Proclaiming His name cancels His greatness
Proclaiming His name asks for rain
medium.explanation: After proclaiming the Lord’s name, Moses calls the listeners to acknowledge His greatness.

medium.question: In “My doctrine shall drop as the rain,” what does “doctrine” mean?
answers: My actions
My teaching or instruction
My land
medium.explanation: Here, doctrine means teaching or instruction, compared to rain that refreshes the earth.

medium.question: How is the Lord described in verse 4?
answers: His ways are hidden
He changes His judgment
He is perfect, faithful, just, and upright
medium.explanation: The verse calls God the Rock and describes His work as perfect and His ways as just.

challenge.question: What can we infer from comparing Moses’ words to rain and dew?
answers: His words should sink in, nourish, and help the hearers grow
His words were meant only to frighten the hearers
His words were spoken only during a storm
challenge.explanation: Rain and dew nourish plants, so the image presents Moses’ words as beneficial and life-giving.

challenge.question: Why are the heavens and earth mentioned together at the beginning?
answers: To identify a place in the wilderness
To show that all creation is called to hear the testimony
To describe the weather
challenge.explanation: The heavens and earth represent all creation, emphasizing the importance and scope of Moses’ words.

challenge.question: What does the title “the Rock” suggest about God in verse 4?
answers: He lives inside a particular rock
He rules only over mountains
He is stable and trustworthy, and His actions are just
challenge.explanation: The image of a rock emphasizes strength and stability, qualities explained by the rest of the verse.

questions.question: What can we infer from comparing Moses’ words to rain and dew?
answers: His words should sink in, nourish, and help the hearers grow
His words were meant only to frighten the hearers
His words were spoken only during a storm
questions.explanation: Rain and dew nourish plants, so the image presents Moses’ words as beneficial and life-giving.

questions.question: Why are the heavens and earth mentioned together at the beginning?
answers: To identify a place in the wilderness
To show that all creation is called to hear the testimony
To describe the weather
questions.explanation: The heavens and earth represent all creation, emphasizing the importance and scope of Moses’ words.

questions.question: What does the title “the Rock” suggest about God in verse 4?
answers: He lives inside a particular rock
He rules only over mountains
He is stable and trustworthy, and His actions are just
questions.explanation: The image of a rock emphasizes strength and stability, qualities explained by the rest of the verse.

paragraphs.title: A Faithless Generation and the Memory of the Ages

easy.question: How is the Lord described in verse 6?
answers: As the people’s Father and Maker
As king of many nations
As an old man recalling the past
easy.explanation: The verse says that God is their Father, Maker, and establisher.

easy.question: Whom does Moses tell the people to ask about the past?
answers: Only the priests
Their father and the elders
The kings of other nations
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Ask thy father … thy elders, and they will tell thee.”

easy.question: What is the Lord’s portion according to verse 9?
answers: All the nations
The wilderness
His people, Jacob
easy.explanation: The verse says, “The Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.”

medium.question: What sequence does verse 7 give for learning from the past?
answers: Remember, consider, then ask the father and elders
Ask, forget, then understand
Fight, win, then remember
medium.explanation: The verse first commands remembrance and reflection, then directs the people to ask their elders.

medium.question: Why are the people called foolish and unwise in verse 6?
answers: They did not know the other nations
They repaid the Lord with evil even though He made them
They failed to ask about territorial boundaries
medium.explanation: They are foolish because they reject the Father and Maker who established them.

medium.question: In “a foolish people and unwise,” what does “foolish” mean?
answers: Lacking good sense or moral understanding
Very wealthy
Living in the wilderness
medium.explanation: The word describes a people lacking wisdom and gratitude, not their wealth or location.

challenge.question: What connection does verse 8 make between the nations and Israel?
answers: The nations set their own boundaries
Israel received all the nations’ borders
The nations’ boundaries were set according to the number of Israel’s children
challenge.explanation: The verse connects the division of the nations with the number of the children of Israel.

challenge.question: What can we infer from “They have corrupted themselves; their spot is not the spot of his children”?
answers: The fault lies in the people’s conduct, not in God
God deliberately corrupted His children
The people have no connection to God
challenge.explanation: The statement places the corruption in the people, not in their Maker.

challenge.question: What does “Jacob is the lot of his inheritance” emphasize?
answers: Jacob’s enslavement to other nations
A defined and special inheritance
A tool for measuring time
challenge.explanation: A lot is a measured share or inheritance, showing Jacob’s special status as God’s portion.

questions.question: What connection does verse 8 make between the nations and Israel?
answers: The nations set their own boundaries
Israel received all the nations’ borders
The nations’ boundaries were set according to the number of Israel’s children
questions.explanation: The verse connects the division of the nations with the number of the children of Israel.

questions.question: What can we infer from “They have corrupted themselves; their spot is not the spot of his children”?
answers: The fault lies in the people’s conduct, not in God
God deliberately corrupted His children
The people have no connection to God
questions.explanation: The statement places the corruption in the people, not in their Maker.

questions.question: What does “Jacob is the lot of his inheritance” emphasize?
answers: Jacob’s enslavement to other nations
A defined and special inheritance
A tool for measuring time
questions.explanation: A lot is a measured share or inheritance, showing Jacob’s special status as God’s portion.

easy.question: Where did the Lord find Israel?
answers: In a desert land
In a great city
By the seashore
easy.explanation: The verse says that He found him in a desert land and a howling wilderness.

easy.question: How did the Lord guard Israel?
answers: Like a bird in its nest
As the apple of His eye
Like fruit in a field
easy.explanation: The verse says that He kept Israel as the apple of His eye.

easy.question: What does the eagle do for its young in the comparison?
answers: Leaves them in the nest
Teaches them to swim
Carries them on its wings
easy.explanation: The eagle spreads its wings, takes its young, and carries them on its wings.

medium.question: What does the eagle image teach about God’s treatment of Israel?
answers: He protects and guides Israel
He immediately punishes Israel
He leaves Israel alone
medium.explanation: As the eagle protects and carries its young, God protects and guides Israel.

medium.question: In “He made him ride on the high places,” what are “high places”?
answers: Valleys
Elevated places
Caves
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to high or elevated places in the land.

medium.question: What is described after God leads Israel?
answers: Israel returns to the wilderness
Israel fights the eagle
Israel enjoys abundant food
medium.explanation: The passage lists produce, honey, oil, milk, meat, and wine.

challenge.question: What do “the Lord alone did lead him” and “there was no strange god with him” emphasize?
answers: The Lord alone was Israel’s leader
Israel was led by many gods
The Lord did not lead Israel
challenge.explanation: The words stress that God alone guided Israel, without any foreign god beside Him.

challenge.question: Which detail shows that abundance came even from unlikely places?
answers: The eagle hovering over its young
Honey from the rock and oil from the flinty rock
The Lord leading Israel alone
challenge.explanation: Honey and oil from rocks picture abundance coming from difficult and unexpected places.

challenge.question: What does “thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape” mean?
answers: Drinking actual blood
Drinking water from grapes
Drinking plentiful, excellent wine
challenge.explanation: “Blood of the grape” is a poetic image for grape juice or wine.

questions.question: What do “the Lord alone did lead him” and “there was no strange god with him” emphasize?
answers: The Lord alone was Israel’s leader
Israel was led by many gods
The Lord did not lead Israel
questions.explanation: The words stress that God alone guided Israel, without any foreign god beside Him.

questions.question: Which detail shows that abundance came even from unlikely places?
answers: The eagle hovering over its young
Honey from the rock and oil from the flinty rock
The Lord leading Israel alone
questions.explanation: Honey and oil from rocks picture abundance coming from difficult and unexpected places.

questions.question: What does “thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape” mean?
answers: Drinking actual blood
Drinking water from grapes
Drinking plentiful, excellent wine
questions.explanation: “Blood of the grape” is a poetic image for grape juice or wine.

easy.question: What did Jeshurun do after becoming prosperous and strong?
answers: Forsook the God who made him
Built the Temple
Returned to his ancestors
easy.explanation: Jeshurun grew fat and strong, then forsook the God who made him.

easy.question: To whom did the Israelites sacrifice?
answers: Angels
Devils that were not God
Prophets
easy.explanation: The verse says they sacrificed to devils, not to God.

easy.question: Whom did the Israelites forget?
answers: Moses
Their ancestors
The God who formed them
easy.explanation: They forgot the God who formed and created them.

medium.question: What connection is made between Jeshurun’s prosperity and forsaking God?
answers: Prosperity led him to become self-confident and reject God
Prosperity made him more grateful
Prosperity made him leave his land
medium.explanation: The passage says that after becoming prosperous, Jeshurun kicked and forsook God.

medium.question: In “thou hast forgotten God that formed thee,” what does “formed” mean?
answers: Protected you
Created you
Ruled your people
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to God as the one who created or shaped His people.

medium.question: What sequence is described in these verses?
answers: Forgetting God, prosperity, then worshiping God
Prosperity, rejecting God, idolatry, and forgetting the Creator
Idolatry, war, then prosperity
medium.explanation: Jeshurun prospers, rejects God, turns to false gods, and forgets his Creator.

challenge.question: What can we infer from calling the idols “new gods that came newly up”?
answers: They were Israel’s ancient ancestral gods
They appeared only after Moses’ time
They were new gods unknown to Israel’s ancestors
challenge.explanation: The phrase stresses that Israel turned to unfamiliar and foreign gods.

challenge.question: Why is the image of “the Rock” fitting for God?
answers: It expresses stability, protection, and salvation
It describes a place where trees grow
It names a sacrificial tool
challenge.explanation: A rock suggests strength and stability, fitting God as Israel’s protector and Savior.

challenge.question: What is the main contrast between God and the idols?
answers: God created and saved, while the idols are not gods
God is new, while the idols are ancient
God is weak, while the idols are strong
challenge.explanation: God is called Israel’s Rock and Creator; the other gods are described as false and foreign.

questions.question: What can we infer from calling the idols “new gods that came newly up”?
answers: They were Israel’s ancient ancestral gods
They appeared only after Moses’ time
They were new gods unknown to Israel’s ancestors
questions.explanation: The phrase stresses that Israel turned to unfamiliar and foreign gods.

questions.question: Why is the image of “the Rock” fitting for God?
answers: It expresses stability, protection, and salvation
It describes a place where trees grow
It names a sacrificial tool
questions.explanation: A rock suggests strength and stability, fitting God as Israel’s protector and Savior.

questions.question: What is the main contrast between God and the idols?
answers: God created and saved, while the idols are not gods
God is new, while the idols are ancient
God is weak, while the idols are strong
questions.explanation: God is called Israel’s Rock and Creator; the other gods are described as false and foreign.

paragraphs.title: Hiding His Face and Returning Their Provocation

easy.question: What did the Lord see that made Him angry with His children?
answers: Their behavior
The land of Israel
Their enemies
easy.explanation: The verse says that the Lord saw their actions and was angered.

easy.question: What did the Lord say He would do to them?
answers: Send them a king
Hide His face from them
Lead them into the wilderness
easy.explanation: He says, “I will hide my face from them.”

easy.question: How did Israel provoke the Lord?
answers: By their wars
By building cities
By their vanities and idolatry
easy.explanation: They provoked Him with what was not God and with their vanities.

medium.question: Why did the Lord say He would hide His face from them?
answers: They were a perverse generation without faith
He could not find them in the land
They asked Him to hide
medium.explanation: Their unfaithful and rebellious behavior led to God’s withdrawal of protection.

medium.question: What does “a very froward generation” mean?
answers: A generation living in many places
A stubborn, rebellious generation
A very happy generation
medium.explanation: The phrase describes people who are crooked, faithless, and rebellious.

medium.question: What connection is made between Israel’s actions and God’s response?
answers: Israel served God, so God blessed them
Israel asked for help, so God hid His face
Israel provoked God, so He would provoke them through another nation
medium.explanation: God responds in kind: because they provoked Him, He would provoke them through a foolish nation.

challenge.question: What can we infer from “I will hide my face” followed by “I will see what their end shall be”?
answers: God withdraws protection but still knows and observes their outcome
God does not know what will happen
God ends His relationship with every nation
challenge.explanation: Hiding His face means withdrawing favor, not ceasing to know what happens to them.

challenge.question: What idea is shared by “that which is not God” and “those which are not a people”?
answers: Both describe the Temple
Both refer to something lacking the proper status or worth
Both refer to Israel
challenge.explanation: Israel chose what was not truly God, and God would use a people regarded as insignificant.

challenge.question: What wordplay appears in God’s response?
answers: God punishes them without mentioning their actions
God hides His face but says nothing about their future
The same root is repeated: they provoked Him, and He will provoke them
challenge.explanation: The verse creates measure for measure through the repeated idea of provoking to anger.

questions.question: What can we infer from “I will hide my face” followed by “I will see what their end shall be”?
answers: God withdraws protection but still knows and observes their outcome
God does not know what will happen
God ends His relationship with every nation
questions.explanation: Hiding His face means withdrawing favor, not ceasing to know what happens to them.

questions.question: What idea is shared by “that which is not God” and “those which are not a people”?
answers: Both describe the Temple
Both refer to something lacking the proper status or worth
Both refer to Israel
questions.explanation: Israel chose what was not truly God, and God would use a people regarded as insignificant.

questions.question: What wordplay appears in God’s response?
answers: God punishes them without mentioning their actions
God hides His face but says nothing about their future
The same root is repeated: they provoked Him, and He will provoke them
questions.explanation: The verse creates measure for measure through the repeated idea of provoking to anger.

easy.question: What was kindled in the Lord’s anger?
answers: Fire
Wind
Water
easy.explanation: The verse says, “For a fire is kindled in mine anger.”

easy.question: What did the Lord say He would heap upon them?
answers: Blessings
Troubles and calamities
Gifts
easy.explanation: He says, “I will heap mischiefs upon them.”

easy.question: What would be outside the house?
answers: The sword
Joy
Rest
easy.explanation: The verse says, “The sword without.”

medium.question: What does “the sword without shall destroy” imply?
answers: It will cause the loss of children and lives
It will bring wealth
It will protect the family
medium.explanation: The sword outside the home represents killing and loss.

medium.question: How do the troubles expand in verses 23–25?
answers: From many troubles to peace
From damage to the land to threats against people everywhere
From war to celebration
medium.explanation: The passage moves from general calamities to hunger, disease, beasts, the sword outside, and terror within.

medium.question: What do the sword outside and terror within show?
answers: Danger exists only on the battlefield
The home is always safe
There is no safe place, outside or inside
medium.explanation: The dangers surround people both outside the home and within it.

challenge.question: What does the fire consuming the earth and burning the mountains’ foundations emphasize?
answers: The immense and widespread power of the destruction
The fire is limited to one house
The mountains become homes
challenge.explanation: The broad images of earth and mountains emphasize destruction on a vast scale.

challenge.question: What does the list “young man … virgin … suckling … man of gray hairs” show?
answers: Only soldiers will suffer
The disaster affects people of every age and sex
Only the elderly will survive
challenge.explanation: The list includes young, old, male, female, and infant, showing that the calamity spares no group.

challenge.question: What sequence stands out in verses 22–25?
answers: Anger and fire, many troubles, hunger and disease, then sword and terror
Peace, abundance, victory, and joy
Sword, blessings, then deliverance
challenge.explanation: The verses progress through an expanding series of disasters, ending with danger outside and inside.

questions.question: What does the fire consuming the earth and burning the mountains’ foundations emphasize?
answers: The immense and widespread power of the destruction
The fire is limited to one house
The mountains become homes
questions.explanation: The broad images of earth and mountains emphasize destruction on a vast scale.

questions.question: What does the list “young man … virgin … suckling … man of gray hairs” show?
answers: Only soldiers will suffer
The disaster affects people of every age and sex
Only the elderly will survive
questions.explanation: The list includes young, old, male, female, and infant, showing that the calamity spares no group.

questions.question: What sequence stands out in verses 22–25?
answers: Anger and fire, many troubles, hunger and disease, then sword and terror
Peace, abundance, victory, and joy
Sword, blessings, then deliverance
questions.explanation: The verses progress through an expanding series of disasters, ending with danger outside and inside.

paragraphs.title: Mercy for the Sake of God’s Name

easy.question: What did the Lord say He might do to the people?
answers: Put an end to their memory
Increase their number
Lead them to a new land
easy.explanation: He says He would make their remembrance cease from among men.

easy.question: Whom did the Lord fear?
answers: Moses
The enemy
The priests
easy.explanation: The passage speaks of the enemy’s wrath and their adversaries.

easy.question: What might the enemies say if they defeated Israel?
answers: The Lord saved them
Our hand is high, and the Lord hath not done all this
Israel is stronger than we are
easy.explanation: The enemies might wrongly claim that their own power brought the victory.

medium.question: Why would the Lord not destroy Israel immediately?
answers: Israel had already won
The enemies would seek peace
The enemies might claim the victory for themselves
medium.explanation: God feared that the enemy would say their own strength, rather than the Lord, had achieved the victory.

medium.question: In “lest I should fear the wrath of the enemy,” what does “fear” mean?
answers: Gather
Be afraid of
Flee
medium.explanation: The phrase means that God is concerned about the enemy’s anger and its consequences.

medium.question: What is the sequence of ideas in these verses?
answers: God considers ending Israel, but fears the enemy will credit themselves
The enemies repent, and God destroys them
Israel wins, then claims God did not act
medium.explanation: The Lord considers scattering Israel but refrains because of what the enemies might claim.

challenge.question: What is the central concern in “lest they should say”?
answers: The enemies will deny their own existence
The enemies will say Israel is stronger
The enemies will credit their success to themselves rather than to God
challenge.explanation: The next words explain the concern: “Our hand is high, and the Lord hath not done all this.”

challenge.question: What does “Our hand is high” reveal about the enemies?
answers: They will see themselves as powerful victors
They will admit their weakness
They will ask Israel for help
challenge.explanation: The expression shows pride and the attribution of success to their own power.

challenge.question: What contrast appears at the end of the verse?
answers: Enemy versus people
Human power versus the Lord’s action
Past versus future
challenge.explanation: The claim “Our hand is high” is contrasted with the truth that the Lord did all this.

questions.question: What is the central concern in “lest they should say”?
answers: The enemies will deny their own existence
The enemies will say Israel is stronger
The enemies will credit their success to themselves rather than to God
questions.explanation: The next words explain the concern: “Our hand is high, and the Lord hath not done all this.”

questions.question: What does “Our hand is high” reveal about the enemies?
answers: They will see themselves as powerful victors
They will admit their weakness
They will ask Israel for help
questions.explanation: The expression shows pride and the attribution of success to their own power.

questions.question: What contrast appears at the end of the verse?
answers: Enemy versus people
Human power versus the Lord’s action
Past versus future
questions.explanation: The claim “Our hand is high” is contrasted with the truth that the Lord did all this.

paragraphs.title: Lack of Understanding and a Lesson for the Future

easy.question: What does the nation lack?
answers: Counsel and understanding
Strength and weapons
Land and water
easy.explanation: The verse calls them a nation without counsel or understanding.

easy.question: What would they understand if they were wise?
answers: How to win a war
Their latter end
Who their kings would be
easy.explanation: They would understand what their final outcome would be.

easy.question: What unusual military ratio is described?
answers: One chases two
One protects a thousand
One chases a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight
easy.explanation: The verse says one could chase a thousand and two could put ten thousand to flight.

medium.question: Why can a few enemies defeat many Israelites?
answers: The Lord sold them and shut them up
They had more weapons
They were wiser
medium.explanation: The verse explains the unusual victory as the Lord’s action against Israel.

medium.question: What is the sequence in verse 29?
answers: They fight, win, and then become wise
If they were wise, they would understand their latter end
They understand their end, then become wise
medium.explanation: The verse presents wisdom as the condition that would lead them to understand their future.

medium.question: What does “their latter end” mean?
answers: Their dwelling place
The beginning of their journey
What will happen to them in the end
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to their final outcome or future.

challenge.question: What can we infer from the gap between one chasing a thousand and two putting ten thousand to flight?
answers: It is an extraordinary victory not explained by ordinary strength
There were a thousand soldiers on each side
The numbers are only a list of names
challenge.explanation: The enormous ratio shows that the victory comes from God, not normal military advantage.

challenge.question: What connection is there between the nation’s lack of understanding and the question in verse 30?
answers: Lack of understanding teaches them warfare
If they understood, they would see that God caused the defeat
Lack of understanding helps them defeat many enemies
challenge.explanation: A wise people would recognize that the Lord had given them into their enemies’ hands.

challenge.question: What does “How should one chase a thousand” express?
answers: A command to begin war
A normal military exercise
A question expressing amazement at an extraordinary situation
challenge.explanation: The question highlights how impossible the result would be unless God had delivered them.

questions.question: What can we infer from the gap between one chasing a thousand and two putting ten thousand to flight?
answers: It is an extraordinary victory not explained by ordinary strength
There were a thousand soldiers on each side
The numbers are only a list of names
questions.explanation: The enormous ratio shows that the victory comes from God, not normal military advantage.

questions.question: What connection is there between the nation’s lack of understanding and the question in verse 30?
answers: Lack of understanding teaches them warfare
If they understood, they would see that God caused the defeat
Lack of understanding helps them defeat many enemies
questions.explanation: A wise people would recognize that the Lord had given them into their enemies’ hands.

questions.question: What does “How should one chase a thousand” express?
answers: A command to begin war
A normal military exercise
A question expressing amazement at an extraordinary situation
questions.explanation: The question highlights how impossible the result would be unless God had delivered them.

easy.question: Whose vine is Israel’s enemies’ vine compared to?
answers: Sodom and Gomorrah
Israel
Egypt
easy.explanation: The verse compares their vine to the vine of Sodom and the fields of Gomorrah.

easy.question: How are the grapes described?
answers: Sweet and healthy
Bitter
Large and beautiful
easy.explanation: Their grapes are called grapes of gall, and their clusters are bitter.

easy.question: What is their wine compared to?
answers: Living water
Sweet honey
The poison of dragons and venom of asps
easy.explanation: The verse portrays their wine as poisonous and dangerous.

medium.question: What does the comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah and poisonous fruit suggest?
answers: Their actions are corrupt and harmful
They are excellent farmers
Their wine is especially fine
medium.explanation: The images of Sodom, bitterness, and poison portray their way as corrupt and dangerous.

medium.question: In “grapes of gall,” what does “gall” mean?
answers: A crown
A bitter poison
The head of the body
medium.explanation: Here, gall means a bitter or poisonous substance.

medium.question: What is the sequence of images in verses 32–33?
answers: Wine, then grapes, then vine
Grapes, then vine, then clusters
Vine, grapes and clusters, then wine
medium.explanation: The image moves from the vine to its fruit and finally to the poisonous wine.

challenge.question: What is emphasized by moving from vine to grapes, clusters, and wine?
answers: The corruption worsens until it produces something dangerous
The fruit becomes sweeter over time
The verse describes only ordinary farming
challenge.explanation: The image begins with a corrupt source, continues through bitter fruit, and ends in poisonous wine.

challenge.question: What does “their rock is not as our Rock” emphasize?
answers: The two rocks are exactly the same
Their power is unlike the strength and power of our Rock
There is no comparison between them
challenge.explanation: The verse clearly contrasts the enemies’ supposed source of strength with Israel’s Rock.

challenge.question: What does “our enemies themselves being judges” suggest?
answers: The enemies became farmers
The enemies drank the wine
Even the enemies can recognize and testify to the difference
challenge.explanation: The enemies themselves can serve as witnesses that their rock is unlike Israel’s Rock.

questions.question: What is emphasized by moving from vine to grapes, clusters, and wine?
answers: The corruption worsens until it produces something dangerous
The fruit becomes sweeter over time
The verse describes only ordinary farming
questions.explanation: The image begins with a corrupt source, continues through bitter fruit, and ends in poisonous wine.

questions.question: What does “their rock is not as our Rock” emphasize?
answers: The two rocks are exactly the same
Their power is unlike the strength and power of our Rock
There is no comparison between them
questions.explanation: The verse clearly contrasts the enemies’ supposed source of strength with Israel’s Rock.

questions.question: What does “our enemies themselves being judges” suggest?
answers: The enemies became farmers
The enemies drank the wine
Even the enemies can recognize and testify to the difference
questions.explanation: The enemies themselves can serve as witnesses that their rock is unlike Israel’s Rock.

paragraphs.title: Judgment Stored Up and the Day of Calamity

easy.question: Where are these things stored?
answers: Among God’s treasures
In the wilderness
In their homes
easy.explanation: The verse says they are sealed up among God’s treasures.

easy.question: To whom do vengeance and recompense belong?
answers: The people
God
The kings
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “To me belongeth vengeance and recompence.”

easy.question: What is near?
answers: A day of joy
A time of rest
The day of their calamity
easy.explanation: The verse says that the day of their calamity is at hand.

medium.question: What is the connection between their slipping foot and the day of calamity?
answers: Their fall is connected with the approaching time of trouble
Their fall cancels the calamity
Their foot slips because of joy
medium.explanation: The verse links their loss of stability with the coming day of judgment.

medium.question: What does “sealed up among my treasures” mean?
answers: Completely forgotten
Kept and hidden
Given to others
medium.explanation: The judgment is stored and concealed until the proper time.

medium.question: What order of events is described?
answers: Vengeance disappears and is then stored
The calamity moves away and their feet grow strong
The judgment is stored, they fall, and the day of calamity approaches
medium.explanation: The verse presents stored judgment, impending collapse, and the nearness of calamity.

challenge.question: What can we infer from “sealed up among my treasures”?
answers: The judgment is preserved for the proper time and will not be canceled
The judgment has already been given to the enemies
God does not know about the judgment
challenge.explanation: The image describes something safely kept until the time it is carried out.

answers: Successful progress
Loss of stability and collapse
Beginning a new journey
challenge.explanation: A slipping foot represents falling, weakness, and loss of security.

challenge.question: What do “the day of their calamity is at hand” and “the things that shall come … make haste” emphasize?
answers: The disaster has already passed
The future is unrelated to their actions
The calamity is near and approaching quickly
challenge.explanation: Both expressions stress the nearness and speed of the coming judgment.

questions.question: What can we infer from “sealed up among my treasures”?
answers: The judgment is preserved for the proper time and will not be canceled
The judgment has already been given to the enemies
God does not know about the judgment
questions.explanation: The image describes something safely kept until the time it is carried out.

answers: Successful progress

questions.explanation: A slipping foot represents falling, weakness, and loss of security.

answers: The disaster has already passed

paragraphs.title: The Lord Judges His People; Idols Cannot Save

easy.question: Whom does the Lord judge?
answers: His people
Their enemies
The priests
easy.explanation: The verse says, “The Lord shall judge his people.”

easy.question: What does the Lord see in the people?
answers: Great wealth
Their power is gone
Victory in war
easy.explanation: The verse says that their power has disappeared.

easy.question: What are the gods of the nations challenged to do?
answers: Eat their sacrifices
Drink their wine
Rise and help them
easy.explanation: The verse challenges these gods to rise up and help.

medium.question: What sequence is described?
answers: The Lord sees their weakness, then asks where their gods are
The people win, then sacrifice to the Lord
Foreign gods help, then the people become weak
medium.explanation: The Lord first sees that their power is gone, and then asks where their gods are.

medium.question: What does “their power is gone” mean?
answers: Their hand became longer
Their strength and ability disappeared
The people raised their hands
medium.explanation: The phrase means that their power has run out.

medium.question: Why mention the fat of sacrifices and the wine of drink offerings?
answers: To describe an ordinary meal
To explain how wine is made
To recall the worship given to the gods they trusted
medium.explanation: The verse recalls the offerings made to the foreign gods and then challenges them to help.

challenge.question: What is the main contrast between the Lord and the other gods?
answers: The Lord responds compassionately to His powerless people, while the others are tested for their ability to help
The Lord eats sacrifices, while the others do not
The Lord drinks wine, while the others drink water
challenge.explanation: The Lord sees His people’s weakness and has compassion, while the idols are shown unable to save.

challenge.question: What does “he shall repent himself for his servants” mean here?
answers: He will forget His servants
He will have mercy on them and restore His favor
He will hide from His servants
challenge.explanation: In context, the phrase means that God will show compassion and act for their good.

challenge.question: What is the purpose of the question “Where are their gods?”
answers: To ask for the gods’ names
To locate the Temple
To test and expose whether those gods can actually save
challenge.explanation: The rhetorical question challenges the idols to prove whether they can protect their worshipers.

questions.question: What is the main contrast between the Lord and the other gods?
answers: The Lord responds compassionately to His powerless people, while the others are tested for their ability to help

questions.explanation: The Lord sees His people’s weakness and has compassion, while the idols are shown unable to save.

answers: To ask for the gods’ names

questions.explanation: The rhetorical question challenges the idols to prove whether they can protect their worshipers.

paragraphs.title: The Lord’s Sovereignty, Judgment, and Vengeance

easy.question: What does the Lord declare about Himself?
answers: There is no god with Him
He needs help
He does not live forever
easy.explanation: He says, “There is no god with me.”

easy.question: Which actions does the Lord name?
answers: Creating heaven and dividing lands
Killing and making alive, wounding and healing
Leading Israel through the wilderness
easy.explanation: He says, “I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal.”

easy.question: What are the nations commanded to do?
answers: Fight Israel
Build an altar
Rejoice with His people
easy.explanation: The verse commands the nations to rejoice with God’s people.

medium.question: What is the connection between “none can deliver out of my hand” and vengeance?
answers: Since no one can stop Him, the Lord can take vengeance on His enemies
The enemies will rescue Israel
The Lord asks His enemies to take vengeance on Him
medium.explanation: God emphasizes that no one can prevent Him from carrying out His judgment.

medium.question: In “I will make mine arrows drunk with blood,” what does “drunk” mean?
answers: Hidden
Filled or soaked
Thrown into the sky
medium.explanation: The image describes arrows saturated with the blood of enemies.

medium.question: What sequence appears in verses 41–43?
answers: God creates the world, then goes to Egypt
Israel leaves Egypt, then receives the Torah
God takes vengeance on enemies, then the nations rejoice and the land and people receive mercy
medium.explanation: The passage moves from judgment and vengeance to rejoicing and mercy for the land and people.

challenge.question: What does “my sword shall devour flesh” emphasize?
answers: The strength and fullness of God’s vengeance
That a sword needs ordinary food
That the war ended without casualties
challenge.explanation: The vivid image emphasizes the power and completeness of divine judgment.

challenge.question: What does “I live for ever” teach about God?
answers: He will die after the war
He is eternal, so His power and promises are not limited by time
He lives only while Israel fights
challenge.explanation: The statement presents God as eternal and permanently able to fulfill His word.

challenge.question: What can we infer from moving from vengeance to mercy for the land and people?
answers: The only goal is to punish enemies
The enemies immediately become Israelites
Judgment also leads to restoration and cleansing
challenge.explanation: The ending includes not only punishment but also mercy, atonement, and restoration.

questions.question: What does “my sword shall devour flesh” emphasize?
answers: The strength and fullness of God’s vengeance

That the war ended without casualties
questions.explanation: The vivid image emphasizes the power and completeness of divine judgment.

answers: He will die after the war

questions.explanation: The statement presents God as eternal and permanently able to fulfill His word.

answers: The only goal is to punish enemies

questions.explanation: The ending includes not only punishment but also mercy, atonement, and restoration.

paragraphs.title: Moses Delivers the Song and Commands the People

easy.question: Who spoke the words of the song to the people?
answers: Moses
Joshua
Aaron
easy.explanation: Moses spoke all the words of the song in the ears of the people.

easy.question: To whom did Moses give these instructions?
answers: The kings of the nations
All Israel
The priests alone
easy.explanation: Moses addressed all Israel.

easy.question: What is said about the words of the law?
answers: They are empty
They are only for Moses
They are your life
easy.explanation: The verse says, “It is your life.”

medium.question: What were the Israelites to do with Moses’ teaching?
answers: Teach their children to observe and do it
Write it only on stones
Hide it from their children
medium.explanation: They were commanded to teach their children to observe and practice all the words of the law.

medium.question: What does “it is not a vain thing for you” mean?
answers: It is something new
It is not empty or worthless
It is a secret matter
medium.explanation: The law is not pointless; it is their life.

medium.question: What connection is made between obeying the law and life in the land?
answers: Obedience will prolong their days in the land
Obedience will keep them from crossing the Jordan
Obedience removes the need to teach their children
medium.explanation: The verse says that obedience will prolong their days in the land they are entering.

challenge.question: Why does Moses tell the people to set their hearts on these words, not merely hear them?
answers: So they will understand their importance and obey them
So they will remember only the song
So they will not need to teach their children
challenge.explanation: Setting the heart on the words implies deep attention and commitment leading to obedience.

challenge.question: Which detail shows that the message is for future generations?
answers: The mention of Joshua
The command to teach their children
The crossing of the Jordan
challenge.explanation: Teaching the children shows that the message extends beyond Moses’ own generation.

challenge.question: What can we infer from the sequence of teaching, attention, and life?
answers: The law is only to be passed on without being practiced
The law matters only before entering the land
Hearing and obeying the law lead to life and long days in the land
challenge.explanation: The sequence connects listening, obedience, and the blessing of life in the land.

answers: So they will understand their importance and obey them

answers: The mention of Joshua

questions.explanation: Teaching the children shows that the message extends beyond Moses’ own generation.

answers: The law is only to be passed on without being practiced

questions.explanation: The sequence connects listening, obedience, and the blessing of life in the land.

paragraphs.title: The Command to Climb Mount Nebo and See the Land

easy.question: Which mountain was Moses commanded to climb?
answers: Mount Nebo
Mount Sinai
Mount Carmel
easy.explanation: The Lord commanded Moses to climb Mount Nebo in the land of Moab.

easy.question: Which land was Moses told to see?
answers: The land of Edom
The land of Canaan
The land of Egypt
easy.explanation: Moses was told to see Canaan, which God was giving to Israel.

easy.question: Which of Moses’ brothers is mentioned?
answers: Joshua
Caleb
Aaron
easy.explanation: The verse mentions Aaron, Moses’ brother, who died on Mount Hor.

medium.question: Why was Moses commanded to climb Mount Nebo?
answers: To see the land of Canaan
To build a city
To fight Moab
medium.explanation: The Lord told Moses to climb the mountain so he could see Canaan.

medium.question: What does “be gathered unto thy people” mean here?
answers: Return alive to his people
Die and join his ancestors
Gather the people for war
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to Moses’ death and joining his ancestors.

medium.question: What sequence is described?
answers: Moses dies, climbs the mountain, then sees the land
Moses sees the land, climbs the mountain, then God speaks
God speaks, Moses climbs and sees the land, then dies
medium.explanation: God speaks first, then Moses climbs and sees the land, and finally dies on the mountain.

challenge.question: What can we infer from Moses seeing Canaan without entering it?
answers: He is a witness to the promised land, but not one who enters it
Canaan was not given to Israel
Moses did not know where Canaan was
challenge.explanation: Moses sees the land God gives Israel, but the command to die on the mountain shows he will not enter it.

challenge.question: What does the mention of Aaron suggest?
answers: Aaron will lead Israel instead of Moses
Moses’ death parallels Aaron’s death on a mountain
Aaron commanded Moses to climb
challenge.explanation: The verse compares Moses’ end with Aaron’s: both die on a mountain and are gathered to their people.

challenge.question: Which geographical detail identifies Mount Nebo?
answers: It is near the Red Sea
It is in Egypt
It is in Moab, opposite Jericho
challenge.explanation: The verse places the mountain in Moab opposite Jericho.

answers: He is a witness to the promised land, but not one who enters it

questions.explanation: Moses sees the land God gives Israel, but the command to die on the mountain shows he will not enter it.

Aaron commanded Moses to climb
questions.explanation: The verse compares Moses’ end with Aaron’s: both die on a mountain and are gathered to their people.

answers: It is near the Red Sea

It is in Moab, opposite Jericho
questions.explanation: The verse places the mountain in Moab opposite Jericho.

paragraphs.title: The Reason for the Punishment and the Land Seen from Afar

easy.question: What will happen to Moses?
answers: He will see the land but not enter it
He will enter the land first
He will return to Egypt
easy.explanation: Moses will see the land but will not go into it.

easy.question: Where did the act leading to the punishment occur?
answers: Mount Sinai
The waters of Meribah-Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin
Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The verse specifically mentions Meribah-Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.

easy.question: What did Moses and Aaron fail to do?
answers: Keep the Sabbath
Leave Egypt
Sanctify the Lord among Israel
easy.explanation: The verse says they did not sanctify the Lord in the midst of the children of Israel.

medium.question: What was the connection between their action and their punishment?
answers: Because they trespassed and did not sanctify God, they would not enter the land
Because they entered the land, they were expelled
Because they refused to see the land, they could not look at it
medium.explanation: The verses connect their failure at Meribah with their exclusion from the land.

medium.question: In “thou shalt see the land before thee,” what does “before thee” mean?
answers: Inside the land
Opposite or in front of you
Under the land
medium.explanation: The phrase means that Moses will see the land from the opposite side, at a distance.

medium.question: What order is given in verse 52?
answers: Moses will see the land but will not enter it
Moses will enter the land and then see it
Moses will neither see nor hear about the land
medium.explanation: The verse first allows Moses to see the land and then states that he will not enter it.

challenge.question: What is the main contrast in verse 52?
answers: The wilderness and Egypt
Seeing the land versus entering it
Moses and the Israelites
challenge.explanation: Moses may see the land, but he may not go into it.

challenge.question: What can we infer from “the land which I give the children of Israel”?
answers: The land is not intended for Israel
The land was given only to Moses
Moses’ punishment does not cancel God’s gift of the land to Israel
challenge.explanation: The land remains Israel’s promised inheritance even though Moses will not enter it.

challenge.question: Why is it significant that the sin occurred “among the children of Israel”?
answers: It happened publicly and affected how the people understood God’s holiness
Israel happened to be in the land at that time
Only Israelites were allowed in the wilderness
challenge.explanation: The wording shows that the act occurred before the people and failed to honor God publicly among them.
